definition: A hidden provision in corporate contracts — often in Axiom or Sterling-Nakamura agreements — that legally dissolves an employee's prior social and familial obligations upon signing, effectively severing them from non-corporate support networks. Often invoked to prevent workers from organizing.
origin: Corporate legal jargon; widely unknown until Diaspora leaks in 2187 made the term public
usage: Corporate attorneys, labor activists, investigative journalists on the Diaspora; cursed by Tier 2-3 workers
example: Nobody told him about the Fracture Clause until his sister tried to reach him through Sterling-Nakamura HR and got a legal cease-and-desist instead.
